draft.title: Aggression in the 1930s
card: Japan
In 1931 Japan's army seized Manchuria, in north-east China, and set up the puppet state of Manchukuo. The League of Nations condemned this in 1933, and Japan simply left the League.
Italy

In 1935 Mussolini's Italy invaded Ethiopia, a member of the League. The League placed limited sanctions on Italy, but they did not cover important goods such as oil, and Italy completed its conquest in 1936.
Germany

Hitler broke the Treaty of Versailles step by step. He rearmed, sent troops into the demilitarised Rhineland in 1936, united with Austria in 1938 and took the Sudetenland and then the rest of Czechoslovakia in 1938 and 1939.

In each case the League and the major powers protested or took weak action, but nobody forced the aggressor to give up what it had taken. Each success showed that further aggression could carry little risk.
draft.remember: Each act of aggression went largely unchecked, and that made the next one easier.

a.q: What was the result of the League of Nations' response to Japan in Manchuria and Italy in Ethiopia?
opts: Both aggressors kept what they had taken
Both aggressors were forced to withdraw
Both aggressors were defeated in war
Both aggressors were expelled and disarmed
a.why: The League condemned Japan and imposed limited sanctions on Italy, but neither step made them give up the land. Japan left the League and Italy completed its conquest, so the League's response was largely ineffective.
a.clue: Think about whether the League's protests changed what happened on the ground.

b.q: Which statement best explains why Hitler's moves from 1936 to 1938 were not stopped?
opts: Earlier aggression had gone unchecked, so he risked little
Britain and France had already declared war on Germany
The League of Nations had put an army into the Rhineland
Germany had never broken the Treaty of Versailles
b.why: Japan and Italy had already gained territory without being forced back, which showed that protests carried little risk. The other options are wrong: war was not declared until 1939, and Germany had broken Versailles by rearming and entering the Rhineland.
b.clue: Look at what happened to Japan and Italy before Hitler moved.

a.best: Both aggressors kept what they had taken

b.best: Earlier aggression had gone unchecked, so he risked little

problems.detail: The why says the earlier cases 'showed that protests carried little risk'. The card says aggression carried little risk. As written, the why gets the logic backwards.

The why says Japan and Italy had 'already gained territory' before Hitler's moves from 1936. Germany remilitarised the Rhineland in March 1936, while Italy's conquest of Ethiopia was still under way (it ended in May 1936). Only Japan's gain was complete by then.

The question asks why Hitler's moves 'were not stopped', which is about how other powers responded. The intended answer explains why Hitler felt he risked little, which is about Hitler's own reasoning. Rewording the question, for example 'why Hitler felt able to act', would match the answer better.
